statement: Java automates local read/write atomicity of byte, char, short, int, float, and Object reference values, but not double and long.
synchronized methods and blocks control atomicity via locks, and the synchronized statement additionally ensures a cache flush/reload.
The Thread class gives very weak guarantees about control and scheduling.
Every Java object possesses exactly one lock, manipulated only via the synchronized keyword.
A synchronized method `void f(){body}` is equivalent to `void f(){ synchronized(this){body} }`.
Scalars such as int are not objects and so can only be locked via their enclosing objects.

Java locks are reentrant: a thread reaching a synchronized region passes if the lock is free or it already holds the lock, and the lock is released after passing as many closing braces as opening braces.
Synchronization has the side effect of clearing locally cached values and forcing reloads from main storage.
A reviewer should require a lock be acquired before use of any field of any object and released after update.
Without locking there are no promises about if or when caches will be flushed or reloaded, which can lead to unsafe or nonsensical execution.
Failing to lock around field access can cause seeing stale values, seeing inconsistent states from out-of-order writes during cache flushes, and seeing incompletely initialized new objects.

The volatile keyword never usefully applies to reference variables because only the reference itself, not the referenced object, is loaded/flushed; synchronization-based constructions should be used instead.
Declaring a mutating method synchronized precludes conflicting interleavings only if all other methods accessing the same field are also synchronized.
condition: all other methods accessing the field are also synchronized

statement: Storage conflicts (read/write and write/write) can cause a method's postcondition to fail under concurrent execution.
Fully synchronized objects (all methods synchronized) are always safe but not always live or efficient, since they process only one request at a time.
In a fully synchronized object every method must be synchronized, because unsynchronized Java methods execute even when the lock is held.
Methods of a fully synchronized object must not suspend or infinitely loop, and must re-establish a consistent state after exceptions.
Holding a lock during a downstream call to a helper object risks safety (helper exceptions), liveness (helper deadlock), and availability (cannot accept new requests during the helper operation).
Rule of thumb (with variants and exceptions): always lock when updating state, and never lock when sending a message; redesign methods to avoid holding locks during downstream calls.
Two synchronized transactional methods that each acquire two object locks in opposite order can deadlock.
Deadlock in transactional methods can be prevented by resource-ordering lock acquisition, for example ordering on Java hash codes.
Every Java Class object has a lock, and both static and instance methods of Singleton classes should synchronize on it.
Synchronization is always needed for accessors of mutable reference variables.
Immutable objects never change state, so actions on them are always safe and live.
Java blank finals enforce most senses of immutability but do not cover objects that eventually latch into a value they then never change from.
Methods dealing only with immutable aspects of an object's state do not require locking.
Locking precludes storage conflicts and invariant failures and can guarantee method atomicity, but introduces potential liveness failures such as deadlock and lockout.

Balking checks state on entry and exits immediately (throwing or returning an error) if not in the right state; in concurrent contexts the host must control the entire check-act sequence because clients cannot preclude state changes between check and act.
Guarding generalizes locking by waiting until an arbitrary state predicate holds; it relies on other threads' actions for progress and is useless in sequential programs.
Busy-wait spin guarding is unsafe (no protection from read/write conflicts) and wasteful (consumes CPU time).
Busy waiting is acceptable only when the conditions latch (once true, never become false) and the threads are known to run on multiple CPUs.
condition: conditions latch and threads are running on multiple CPUs

statement: A guarded wait must recheck its condition in a while loop upon resumption rather than using a single if test.
Monitor methods wait, notify, and notifyAll can only be invoked while holding the synchronization lock of the target object.
wait() suspends the calling thread, places it in the target object's wait set, and releases the target's synchronization lock.
A notified thread must re-acquire the target's synchronization lock before resuming at its wait point; notifyAll chooses all waiting threads whereas notify chooses one.
Every wait relies on a balancing notification, generating programmer obligations to issue that notification.
Java does not guarantee fairness, so a thread can starve by being continually placed behind others in the queue.
wait(ms) does not by itself indicate whether it returned because of notification or timeout, so code must check for both.
Timeouts are useful for heuristic detection of failures but cannot be used for high-precision timing or deadlines, because time can elapse between wait and thread resumption.
Nested monitor lockout occurs when a thread waits inside a hidden contained object while the enclosing object's lock is retained, so no other thread can ever unblock it.
Never wait on a hidden contained object in Java while holding a lock.

For containment, outermost objects must synchronize access (else thread-caching problems), inner code must be communication-closed with no unprotected calls in or out, and outer objects must never leak the identities of inner objects.
When revealing internal state, copies of mutable inner objects (such as java.awt.Point) must be made because their fields remain mutable.
Splitting independent state subsets onto separate helper/lock objects lets independent actions (such as grow and shift) execute simultaneously and reduces lock contention.
Splitting interdependent fields (for example x and y into an immutable XY value) avoids interleavings in which a reader observes an old x with a new y.
In optimistic update techniques all actions before commit must be reversible, performing no I/O or thread construction unless safely cancellable, so failures are clean.
Optimistic retry loops can livelock unless proven wait-free in the given context.
A two-lock concurrent queue lets puts and polls run concurrently but disallows multiple simultaneous puts or polls, and poll may return null (a balking policy) if another thread is mid-put.
Thread priorities range from 1 to 10, a new thread inherits its creator's priority, and the JVM gives higher-priority threads preference only vaguely and implementation-dependently.
Priorities can only be used heuristically; there is no guarantee that the highest-priority or longest-waiting threads acquire locks or receive notifications before others.
Thread-specific storage suits variables that apply per-activity rather than per-object, is normally preferable to static variables, and can eliminate the need for locking.
In Thread-per-Message, sendMessage should be synchronized when the handler or process arguments are not fixed/final, copying their values to locals under synchronization.
condition: handler reference or process arguments are not fixed/final

statement: Pass-through designs are fragile because there is no opposite to synchronized, so self-calls to a reactive method from synchronized methods should be avoided.

Channel choice involves trade-offs: unbounded queues can exhaust resources if clients outpace handlers, bounded buffers can block clients when full, and synchronous channels force the client to wait for the handler to finish.
AWT uses a single event-dispatch thread and a single EventQueue, and all drawing (update/paint) is performed by the AWT thread, not the application's threads.
The most conservative AWT policy is to perform all GUI-related state updates in event-handling methods and not rely on the thread-safety of GUI components.
In AWT reactive methods one must not hold locks when sending messages and must not block or delay the AWT thread.

Thread pools are often faster than thread-per-message but slower than a single thread working off a multislot buffer unless handler actions permit parallelism, and they work well for I/O-bound actions.
Observer change-notifications must use a oneway design, otherwise notification and current-value callbacks can deadlock against each other.
Thread.stop was deprecated because it stops a thread by throwing ThreadDeath asynchronously, which can corrupt object state by leaving invariants violated mid-method.

Asynchronous cancellation is impractical because safely guarding against it would require catching ThreadDeath after nearly every line, and most thread systems including POSIX do not support or severely restrict it.
The best-supported cancellation policy is that Thread.isInterrupted() means cancelled; any method sensing interruption should assume its task is cancelled and exit as quickly and cleanly as possible.
A method sensing interruption must ensure callers are made aware, either by re-asserting Thread.currentThread().interrupt() or by throwing InterruptedException.
The static Thread.interrupted() clears the current thread's interrupt status and returns its previous value, whereas thread.isInterrupted() returns the status without clearing it.
Threads blocked waiting for synchronized method or block entry are not awakened by interrupt.

InterruptedException is thrown by Thread.sleep, Thread.join, and Object.wait when interrupted while blocked (also clearing status), and blocking java.io methods respond to interrupt by throwing InterruptedIOException.
Cancellation should be checked as a precondition for methods and in the loop headers of looping methods.
Multiphase cancellation first interrupts and joins with a timeout, then escalates (deny security checks, lower priority, last-resort stop) when a thread does not respond to graceful cancellation.
Applet-created threads should be explicitly cancellable (normally in Applet.stop), since otherwise their lifecycle is unpredictable and there is no guarantee browsers kill them on unload.
An ownership-transfer policy keeps at most one stage referring to any resource at a time by nulling out instance variables that refer to a resource after handing it off.
Push flow systems with common directionality and locality constraints preclude many safety and liveness problems, with adherence to design rules potentially formally checkable.
Using a second thread for a stage's second output (as in a Cloner) maintains liveness.
A CyclicBarrier is initialized with the number of members and its barrier call waits for the count to reach zero before resetting to the initial count, supporting iterative group algorithms.
Before/After control wraps an action as pre(); try{action();} finally{post();}, and the control code (execution state) must be separable from the ground action code (intrinsic state).
A latch is a condition that starts false and, once set true, remains true forever, useful for initialization flags, end-of-stream conditions, and thread termination.
A count-based barrier monotonically decrements its count on each release, and all acquires pass when the count reaches zero.
Conditional locking via Sync.attempt enables back-offs, lock reordering, and heuristic deadlock detection through time-outs.

State tracking issues notifications only on state transitions that can unblock another thread, yielding faster but more fragile code with fewer notification calls and harder-to-change guard conditions.
notifyAll wakes all waiting threads even those whose conditions cannot hold, so notify should replace notifyAll only when all threads wait on the same condition and at most one could continue anyway.
condition: all threads wait on the same condition and at most one could proceed

statement: Mixed-condition problems, where threads wait in different methods of the same object for different reasons such as not-Empty versus not-Full, can be resolved by isolating waits and notifications into different objects (splitting).

The inheritance anomaly arises when a subclass guard can block indefinitely because the superclass only notifies on one state transition; most such anomalies are avoided by fine-grained factoring of notification conditions into overridable methods.
Concurrent safety is an extended sense of type safety that adds a temporal dimension and is not completely enforceable by compilers.
Concurrent code has more stringent correctness criteria than sequential code, is usually not automatically statically checkable, and its nondeterminism impedes debuggability and understandability.
Concurrency can be expensive: synchronization, context switching, and scheduling add overhead, and performance profiles may vary across platforms.

Safe objects perform method actions only when in consistent states, because acting in temporarily inconsistent states yields unpredictable consequences such as read/write and write/write conflicts and invariant failures.
